arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (`el registro de decisiones la política de trazado`). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:81503.texto: Man and beast intertwine to form a single writhing body in this emotionally charged depiction of a lion attacking a horse and its rider. Through short, energetic brushstrokes and carefully manipulated contrasts of light and shadow, Eugène Delacroix imbued this imagined scene with action and drama. While many artists of the period explored the theme of man versus nature, depictions of Arab men entangled with wild animals served a specific propagandistic function, justifying the brutality of French colonial rule by depicting its subjects as violent and inhuman.
aic:81503.title: Arab Horseman Attacked by a Lion

cma:109507.texto:
Barbarigo served as second in command of the Venetian naval forces during the Battle of Lepanto, fighting against the Ottoman Empire on October 7, 1571. During the skirmish, Barbarigo was slain by a Turkish arrow, which he holds in the portrait.

Barbarigo’s identity is defined by his military prowess. In the 1500s, Venetian military portraits often portrayed the sitter in armor in a pose typical of a Roman emperor, creating a link to the valor and might of ancient armies.

cma:134620.texto:
Is this painting by Titian?

Titian, the celebrated and prolific 16th-century Venetian artist, and his large workshop painted several versions of this subject. Further research is needed to compare this painting with versions in Milan and Madrid to determine how much of each is by Titian himself, as opposed to being the work of his studio assistants. The Prado Museum in Madrid is often considered to have a copy made from Cleveland’s painting, which is superior in execution but not condition. Despite the damage caused by overcleaning, there are many fine passages, including the bowing white horse, his groom in shadow, and the cradled Christ child.

cma:140149.texto: These panels depicting Saints Anthony the Abbot and Michael originally flanked a central scene of the Madonna and Child with Angels, now lost, to form a triptych. Giovanni di Cosimo de’Medici of Florence commissioned the ensemble in 1457 as a gift to Alfonso V of Aragon. Fra Filippo Lippi, a Carmelite friar and one of the great masters of early Renaissance Florence, depicted realistic, weighty figures in a three-dimensional space using a system of linear perspective, inspired partly by Masaccio’s Brancacci Chapel, and reflected in the background architecture. Saint Anthony the Abbot rejected all earthly possessions in pursuit of a contemplative life in the desert. He is generally regarded as the founder of monasticism and is depicted wearing a monk’s habit. Saint Michael’s sword and shield refer to his role as heaven’s defender against evil.

cma:153773.texto: This painting is a sketch for a large altarpiece. The rough, flickering surface, the unusually sharp contrast of hot and cool hues, and the compression of space all characterize the artist’s intense spirituality and unique technique. While often held apart from the sweetness and grace of Murillo (also represented in the collection), his contemporary in Seville, the two artists worked closely together on commissions and often presented their work side by side, speaking to the stylistic diversity and religious complexity preferred by patrons in Seville during the late 1600s.

The Prado Museum in Madrid is often considered to have a copy made from Cleveland’s painting, which is superior in execution but not condition. Despite the damage caused by overcleaning, there are many fine passages, including the bowing white horse, his groom in shadow, and the cradled Christ child.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1957.150 · CC0 1.0

5. **Study for "The Assumption of the Virgin" for San Augustín, Seville**
   Juan de Valdés Leal · c. 1670–72 · oil on wood
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1987.7

   La obra es un estudio para un gran retablo que se caracteriza por una superficie rugosa y un contraste agudo entre tonos cálidos y fríos, reflejando la intensa espiritualidad del artista. [1]
   La paleta muestra un contraste fuerte y una compresión del espacio que puede interpretarse como un uso de tonos más oscuros y dramáticos en comparación con escenas más suaves.
   No se indica que represente la misma escena que la imagen proporcionada.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “This painting is a sketch for a large altarpiece. The rough, flickering surface, the unusually sharp contrast of hot and cool hues, and the compression of space all characterize the artist’s intense spirituality and unique technique. While often held apart from the sweetness and grace of Murillo (also represented in the collection), his contemporary in Seville, the two artists worked closely together on commissions and often presented their work side by side, speaking to the stylistic diversity and religious complexity preferred by patrons in Seville during the late 1600s.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1987.7 · CC0 1.0
